proposedTopics.title: Huff jump tables & when Huff pays off
proposedTopics.description: Huff builds function dispatch by hand: read the selector with `0x00 calldataload 0xe0 shr`, compare `dup1 __FUNC_SIG(f) eq`, and `jumpi` to each terminating handler. An unmatched selector needs an explicit fallback or revert; otherwise execution falls through into the next label. Manual bytecode can optimize a known interface, but the author owns every control-flow and stack-safety decision.

proposedTopics.title: The 4-byte function selector
proposedTopics.description: A function selector is the first 4 bytes of keccak256 of the canonical signature string — `bytes4(keccak256("transfer(address,uint256)")) == 0xa9059cbb` — using canonical types (`uint256`, not `uint`), no argument names, and no spaces. External-call calldata is this selector followed by ABI-encoded arguments. The 32-bit selector space permits collisions, which matters especially when proxy and implementation interfaces overlap.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase08/Selector.sol compute a selector in Solidity and cross-check with `cast sig "transfer(address,uint256)"`; record three signatures and their selectors in test/phase08/Selector.t.sol. Done when: forge test asserts your computed bytes4 equals the expected value and you can explain why `uint` vs `uint256` in the string breaks it.

proposedTopics.title: The dispatcher jump table
proposedTopics.description: Compiler-generated runtime code first rejects calldata shorter than 4 bytes, then can extract a selector with `shr(0xe0, calldataload(0))`, compare it with function selectors, and jump to the matching body. The exact comparison tree and opcodes are compiler-version, pipeline, optimizer, and interface dependent, so they must be read from the actual deployed-bytecode output rather than assumed.

Done when: the annotations map all three selectors and explicitly record the compiler version and optimizer settings instead of generalizing the observed dispatcher shape.

proposedTopics.title: Calldata layout, fallback & receive at bytecode level
proposedTopics.description: Function-call calldata is a 4-byte selector followed by ABI head/tail encoding: static values are encoded in place, while a dynamic head word points to its tail. Empty calldata routes to `receive()` when present; otherwise a matching payable `fallback()` may handle it. Any calldata with no matching function selector routes to `fallback()` when present. Proxies use that unmatched-call path to delegate.

proposedTopics.title: Sequential slot assignment & struct packing
proposedTopics.description: With the default layout base, Solidity assigns statically sized state variables from slot 0 in C3-linearized inheritance order. Value types use only their needed bytes and pack into a slot from the lower-order bytes when they fit; structs and arrays start a new slot, and their members or elements then follow packing rules. Constants and immutables do not occupy storage slots. Upgrade implementations must preserve the existing layout.

Done when: you can predict which variables share a slot and explain why reordering them is fatal to a delegatecall/upgradeable contract.

proposedTopics.title: Mapping & dynamic-array slot derivation
proposedTopics.description: For a mapping based at slot `p`, key `k` starts at `keccak256(h(k) . p)`: `h` pads value-type keys to 32 bytes but uses unpadded data for `bytes` and `string` keys. Nested mappings apply the rule recursively. A dynamic array normally stores its length at `p`, with data from `keccak256(p)`; 32-byte elements use `keccak256(p) + i`, while smaller elements can pack. Short `bytes` and `string` values are a separate in-slot encoding.

Done when: forge test passes and you can explain why a short `string`/`bytes` (≤31 bytes) is the exception that packs into slot p itself.

proposedTopics.title: ERC-7201 namespaced storage
proposedTopics.description: ERC-7201 documents a storage namespace as an annotated struct rooted at `keccak256(abi.encode(uint256(keccak256(bytes(id))) - 1)) & ~bytes32(uint256(0xff))`. The subtract-one location is outside Solidity's ordinary tree, the second hash keeps a multi-slot namespace disjoint under the stated assumptions, and the mask aligns the root to 256 slots. The annotation is not compiler-enforced, so code must use the claimed root correctly and namespace IDs must not collide.

proposedTopics.title: EIP-1167 minimal-proxy runtime bytecode
proposedTopics.description: ERC-1167 specifies a 45-byte deployed runtime that copies calldata, delegatecalls a fixed 20-byte implementation with all gas, copies returndata, and returns or reverts with it. The ERC explicitly does not standardize deployment bytecode. Because a clone runs the implementation in the clone's storage context, the implementation constructor does not initialize clone state; initialization must be performed explicitly and atomically enough to prevent takeover.

proposedTopics.title: Metamorphic contracts
proposedTopics.description: CREATE2 derives an address from the deployer, salt, and init-code hash, not directly from the runtime returned by that init code. Before EIP-6780, a multi-transaction pattern could delete code with `SELFDESTRUCT` and reuse the same CREATE2 inputs while mutable init-code dependencies returned different runtime. Under EIP-6780, `SELFDESTRUCT` outside the creation transaction transfers balance but does not delete code or storage, so that classic redeployment cycle no longer works.

Done when: the artifact distinguishes init code from runtime code and states the same-creation-transaction exception without claiming same-transaction destroy-and-recreate is possible.

proposedTopics.title: Symbolic execution vs fuzzing
proposedTopics.description: Fuzzing runs sampled concrete inputs and can demonstrate a counterexample but not exhaust the input domain. Symbolic execution represents inputs symbolically, forks on path conditions, and asks a solver whether an assertion can fail; a completed, sound run can establish the property for the modeled domain. Path explosion, timeouts, unsupported behavior, abstractions, and explicit bounds can leave paths unproven, so `no counterexample` is not by itself a proof result.

Done when: you can state one property fuzzing can only sample but symbolic execution can prove, and why 'no counterexample' from a bounded symbolic run is not a full proof.

proposedTopics.title: Certora Prover & CVL

Rules assume their `require` clauses and check assertions; invariants require a constructor base case and preservation by every included state-changing method. The Certora Prover reports verified properties or counterexample traces, but over-strong assumptions, filters, reverting invariant expressions, and unresolved-call modeling can weaken or make an invariant proof unsound.

proposedTopics.title: Writing a verifiable invariant proof
proposedTopics.description: A contract invariant is a precise state predicate expected in every reachable state. An inductive proof establishes it after construction, assumes it before an arbitrary included state-changing method, and proves the method preserves it. The claim is only as broad as the methods, external-call model, and assumptions included; filtering a transition or adding unjustified preserved assumptions can make a reported result unsound.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: Huff jump tables & when Huff pays off
proposedPrompts.promptText: How does a hand-written Huff dispatcher route a call, and what must not be forgotten?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Load the selector (calldataload(0), shr 0xe0), then for each function `dup1 __FUNC_SIG(f) eq <label> jumpi`, else fall through to a revert. Pitfall: omit the final fallback revert and an unknown selector falls into the first function's body — the manual control that makes Huff cheap also makes this your responsibility.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: Huff jump tables & when Huff pays off
proposedPrompts.promptText: In 10 minutes, sketch selector dispatch to two Huff macros and the fallback path. State the stack contract at each jump and one measured reason to keep Solidity instead.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Extract the four-byte selector, compare and jump only to valid labels; consume temporary values and keep each entry/exit stack shape explicit. Compare deployed size and end-to-end gas for the same compiler/EVM target.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How is a function selector computed, and what breaks it?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: bytes4(keccak256(canonicalSignature)) — first 4 bytes of the keccak of e.g. "transfer(address,uint256)" (= 0xa9059cbb), using canonical types, no names, no spaces. Pitfall: writing "uint" instead of "uint256", adding spaces, or including argument names hashes to the wrong selector; 4 bytes also means collisions exist.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the Solidity expression for the selector of transfer(address,uint256).
proposedPrompts.answerHint: bytes4(keccak256("transfer(address,uint256)")) == 0xa9059cbb — canonical signature string, first 4 bytes of the keccak256.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does the compiled dispatcher extract and route the selector?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A generated dispatcher can guard calldatasize < 4, use shr(0xe0, calldataload(0)) to right-align the selector, compare selectors, and jump to a matching body; no match follows the generated fallback/receive/revert path. Pitfall: the exact comparison tree depends on compiler version, pipeline, optimizer, and interface, so infer it from the pinned build's disassembly, not a universal heuristic.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the two-op sequence that extracts the selector from calldata.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: shr(0xe0, calldataload(0)) — load the first 32 bytes of calldata and shift right by 224 bits to leave the 4-byte selector right-aligned.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: Calldata layout, fallback & receive at bytecode level
proposedPrompts.promptText: Which of receive/fallback runs for empty vs unmatched calldata?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Empty calldata with receive() present → receive(); if receive is absent, a payable fallback may handle it. Any calldata whose selector matches no function (including non-empty data shorter than 4 bytes) → fallback() when present. Pitfall: fallback must be payable to accept value; proxies deliberately use the unmatched-call path to delegate.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does solc assign storage slots, and what is fatal for an upgradeable contract?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: With the default base, variables follow C3-linearized order from slot 0; value types pack into lower-order bytes when they fit, while structs and arrays start a new slot and pack internally. Constants and immutables use no storage slot. Pitfall: an upgrade must preserve existing layout; reordering, changing types, or inserting before existing fields can reinterpret proxy state.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Where does mapping value m[k] (m at slot p) and dynamic-array element i live?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: m[k] starts at keccak256(h(k) . p): h pads value-type keys to 32 bytes but uses raw unpadded data for bytes/string keys; nested mappings hash recursively. A dynamic array normally stores length at p and data from keccak256(p); 32-byte element i is at base+i, while smaller elements can pack. Short bytes/string (≤31 bytes) store data and length in p itself.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write assembly that computes the storage slot of mapping entry m[key], m at slot p.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: For a `mapping(uint256 => ...)`: assembly { mstore(0x00, key) mstore(0x20, p) let s := keccak256(0x00, 0x40) } — the two mstores produce padded key ‖ slot. For bytes/string keys, h(k) is the raw unpadded key data, so this fixed 64-byte kernel does not apply unchanged.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What problem does ERC-7201 solve, and how is its base slot derived?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It roots an annotated module struct at keccak256(abi.encode(uint256(keccak256(bytes(id))) − 1)) & ~bytes32(uint256(0xff)). The subtract-one seed is outside the ordinary tree, the second hash keeps the multi-slot namespace disjoint under the ERC's assumptions, and the mask aligns to 256 slots. Pitfall: the annotation is not enforced; unique IDs and correct assembly slot assignment remain the author's job.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the ERC-7201 base-slot computation for a namespace string.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: bytes32 slot = keccak256(abi.encode(uint256(keccak256(bytes("my.namespace"))) - 1)) & ~bytes32(uint256(0xff)); — hash the namespace, subtract 1, ABI-encode+hash, clear the low byte.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What is an EIP-1167 clone's runtime, and why can't it be upgraded or run a constructor?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: ERC-1167 standardizes a fixed 45-byte deployed runtime that copies calldata, delegatecalls a fixed 20-byte implementation with all gas, and returns or reverts with returndata; deployment bytecode is explicitly outside the ERC. Pitfall: the implementation constructor never initializes clone storage, so deploy and initialize safely—an uninitialized clone may be taken over.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Give the EIP-1167 runtime bytecode template with the implementation placeholder.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: 363d3d373d3d3d363d73<20-byte-impl>5af43d82803e903d91602b57fd5bf3 — 45 bytes: calldatacopy, delegatecall to <impl> with all gas, returndatacopy, then RETURN on success or REVERT.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Where does an ERC-1967 proxy store the implementation address, and why the odd slot?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: At bytes32(uint256(keccak256("eip1967.proxy.implementation")) − 1) = 0x360894…382bbc, with sibling beacon and optional admin slots; the fallback can sload it and delegatecall. The label hash and −1 convention avoid compiler-allocated state. Pitfall: the slot does not provide upgrade authorization or implementation-layout compatibility—both must be enforced separately.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the constant for the ERC-1967 implementation slot and how the proxy reads it.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: bytes32 constant SLOT = 0x360894a13ba1a3210667c828492db98dca3e2076cc3735a920a3ca505d382bbc; // = keccak256('eip1967.proxy.implementation') - 1; read via sload(SLOT) then delegatecall.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How did metamorphic contracts work, and how did EIP-6780 stop them?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: CREATE2 pins an address to deployer, salt, and init-code hash, while init code may return runtime obtained from mutable dependencies. Pre-6780, code could be deleted in one transaction and different runtime redeployed later with the same CREATE2 inputs. EIP-6780 leaves code/storage intact for later-transaction SELFDESTRUCT. The same-creation-transaction exception still cannot destroy and recreate at that address within one transaction because creation collision rules apply.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What can symbolic execution prove that fuzzing cannot, and what is its main limit?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Fuzzing samples concrete inputs and can find a counterexample but does not exhaust the domain. Symbolic execution forks on symbolic path conditions and can prove an assertion for the modeled domain when every relevant path is discharged, or produce a counterexample. Pitfall: bounds, abstractions, unsupported behavior, path explosion, and timeouts may yield an incomplete run—'no counterexample' alone is not proof.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does Halmos turn a Foundry test into a proof, and what should you watch?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Halmos symbolically executes check_ parameters over their types after setUp and can report assertion counterexamples; svm cheatcodes add symbolic values. Pitfall: dynamic arrays need fixed chosen lengths, vm.assume narrows the domain, and non-assertion reverts are ignored by default. A PASS must be stated with those setup, domain, timeout, and supported-semantics boundaries.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does a CVL spec contain, and how can a spec falsely 'verify'?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A .spec can declare method summaries, rules over symbolic env/args, and invariants. Rules check assertions under their requires; invariants prove a constructor base case and preservation by included state-changing methods. Pitfall: over-strong requires, filtered methods, reverting invariant expressions, preserved assumptions, or unresolved-call modeling can exclude real behavior or make an invariant result unsound.

proposedPrompts.promptText: In 10 minutes, state one CVL rule for an authorized balance transfer and one assumption that could make a passing proof vacuous. How would you detect the bad assumption?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Specify preconditions, state before/after, and conservation. An impossible require or over-constrained environment can hide all executions; inspect reachability and a deliberate mutation.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What makes Kontrol's guarantees strong, and what remains your responsibility?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Kontrol compiles Foundry artifacts into KEVM helper modules and symbolically executes selected Solidity tests against KEVM's K semantics. `build`, `prove`, `list`, and KCFG inspection expose the workflow and proof state. Pitfall: storage abstractions, bounds, lemmas, loop invariants, or manual steps become part of the claim; any open or stuck branch remains unproven, not safe.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What makes an invariant genuinely proven rather than just tested?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Use induction over reachable states: prove the constructor establishes the invariant, then assume it before an arbitrary included state-changing method and prove that method preserves it. Repeat for the complete transition set. Pitfall: filtering a method, adding an unjustified preserved require, allowing the invariant expression to revert, or under-modeling external calls can make a reported result unsound.
